slides.headline: Its heart can slow to 2 beats a minute.
slides.sub: What happened when scientists tagged the largest animal on Earth

slides.label: the lowest heart rate measured in a diving blue whale
slides.body: During foraging dives as deep as 184 m and as long as 16.5 minutes, beats typically ran at just 4–8 a minute.

slides.headline: Compare that with yours
slides.body: A resting adult human heart beats 60–100 times a minute. At its slowest, the diving whale's heart beat 30 to 50 times slower.

slides.headline: Then it races at the surface
slides.body: Between dives, as the whale breathed, its heart sped up to 25–37 beats a minute, near the estimated maximum possible for a heart that size.

slides.headline: A heart of nearly 400 pounds
slides.body: One preserved blue whale heart weighs nearly 400 lb (about 180 kg) and stands about 6.5 ft tall with its main vessels attached.

slides.headline: The largest animal on Earth
slides.body: Up to 110 ft (about 33 m) long and 330,000 lb. Still Endangered (IUCN, 2018), with an estimated 5,000–15,000 mature adults, and increasing.

slides.headline: Save this for the next time your heart races.
slides.body: All of this came from one tagged whale and 8.5 hours of heartbeats. Follow @earthspirit_nature.
sources: Goldbogen, J.A. et al. (2019) Extreme bradycardia and tachycardia in the world's largest animal. PNAS 116:25329–25332
Smithsonian Magazine (2017): preserving a blue whale heart

caption:
A blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus) diving to feed can slow its heart to just 2 beats a minute.

Scientists fixed a suction-cup ECG tag to a single free-diving blue whale in Monterey Bay, California, and recorded 8.5 hours of heartbeats. During each feeding lunge at depth, its heart rate rose about 2.5-fold before slowing again. Their paper's title sums it up: extreme bradycardia and tachycardia in the world's largest animal.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Goldbogen et al. (2019), PNAS 116:25329–25332; NOAA Fisheries; IUCN Red List (2018).
